summary: Gannet Rock light, 13 km south of Grand Manan: an 1831 timber tower, a 1905 second-order lens, keepers until 1996, and the 1899 Castilian grounding in fog.

structures.note: 41 ft 6 in base to vane when built; raised in 1905 on a 12 ft concrete wall to 27.4 m base of wall to vane
5-inch diaphone; horn 37 ft above high water pointing due south
Rebuilt 1906 and again 1930 or 1931; attached to the tower

access.note: Grounds and tower closed; best seen from the water.

events.note: Timber octagonal tower and keeper's dwelling; LighthouseFriends gives the contract payments
First lit December 1831 with red glass
Red glass replaced by white; 11 s light and 9 s dark, worked by a weight-driven shade
12 ft granite wall built round the tower
Fourth-order Fresnel lens and new lantern; first lit 1 August 1867
Saxby Gale; station buildings nearly swept away; repairs of $253
Schooner Gertrude E. Smith ran ashore; all hands saved
Allan liner Castilian ashore in dense fog on 12 March 1899; all saved
Yarmouth life-boat crew helped the barquentine Argentine off the Gannet Rock ledge
Flash pattern changed; total period 40 seconds
Illuminant changed from coal oil to three-mantle incandescent petroleum vapour
Tower raised on a 12 ft concrete wall; new circular iron lantern
Second-order lens giving a double quick flashing light
5-inch diaphone in a new fog-alarm building
Telephone cable laid from Gannet Rock to Little Wood Island
Steamer Gerald Turnbull stranded on Gannet Rock ledge; recorded as a total loss
Lumber schooner Dornfontein looted and fired by a submarine off the mouth of the Bay of Fundy
Old lantern and Fresnel lens removed; temporary tower; new lantern with modern beacon
Last keeper, Barry S. Bagley, left in April 1996
Light solarized; attached dwelling gutted

notes_for_editor: Roster and 1831 to 1904 keeper names other than Dalzell rest on LighthouseFriends (facts only; copyrighted site, one-sentence quotes at most). Dalzell's appointment (1 July 1904, Gannet Rock and Explosive Signal Station) is matched by column position in the Department's keeper table (1906v40 printed p. 260, scan p. 341). The name, station and date columns run in the same order (11 entries, Dickson to Dakin), and the 1904 and 1907 volumes pair Dalzell, Coleman Grant with the same station. The page image (scan p. 341, printed p. 260) was read by the fact-checker: the row reads 'Dalzell, Coleman, Grant' against 'Gannet Rock and Explosive Signal Station', appointed 'July 1, 1904', salary $700.00, so the pairing is confirmed. Sydney W. Tatton is not in the Department's keeper tables for this station; a George T. Tatton appears at Long Eddy Point, so check before publishing. LighthouseFriends disagrees with itself: its keeper list ends Walter B. McLaughlin in 1879 and Oliver A. Kent starts in 1879, but its text says McLaughlin was transferred in 1880; W. Lincoln Harvey starts 1897 in the list and 1898 in his daughter's recollection. A Henry McLaughlin kept Gannet Rock 1843 to 1853 and Head Harbour 1872 to 1879 in LighthouseFriends; not linked. The 1869 Saxby Gale and 1883 Gertrude E. Smith rest on LighthouseFriends alone: the Department's 1870 report is not in the corpus and no Chronicling America hit was found. The Dornfontein's date (Friday 2 August 1918) is supported by the Tribune's own list on the same page ('Aug. 2. Dornfontein (British schooner)'); LighthouseFriends' maiden-voyage and keeper account is not in the Tribune text read. The 1913 Gerald Turnbull wreck line is in the Yarmouth port warden's return (scan p. 302), not in the Department's list of investigations (scan p. 183, which records only 'On May 19, stranded on Gannet dry ledge'), so the story now names the port warden. Unresolved: the federal statement names John Cunningham as designer, while LighthouseFriends records him as a surveyor; a 1921-22 table line about a 4th-order lens (Digby Gut, Gannet rock, Grand passage column block) is ambiguous and is left out; a 1912-13 table line 'Purchase of lighthouse site' is also a column block and left out; the 1834 flashing-light date in a secondary reference (citing Lorimer 1876) is unchecked. The 1991 heritage date in the record is not confirmed: the statement cites a 1990 federal review (FHBRO Report 90-112). The 2010 'surplus' declaration is not checked. Elsie Clark is quoted from LighthouseFriends, not from the interview; she is not a keeper and is left off the roster. The record's light values (Oc W 3s, 12.9 m, 11 nm) match the North light in the current Coast Guard list; the main tower carries a Racon and no separate light entry.
